slots.title: Berkshire EPS $10.33 Beats $5.88 Estimate
slots.body:
$BKR-B class reported EPS of $10.33 for the quarter that ended Nov. 7.

The Street had penciled in about $5.88 per share — the print came in roughly 76% above that figure.

Revenue landed at $105.6 billion versus a consensus near $100.96 billion.

Class A shares ($BRK-A) showed the same revenue line and EPS of $15,502 against an estimate near $8,822.

Both share classes trade on the NYSE; market cap in the release is on the order of $1.22 trillion.

That is operating results from Berkshire’s insurance, railroad, energy, and equity portfolio — not a macro print, but it is one of the largest balance sheets in the U.S. reporting the same morning as the post-election narrative.

Which line matters more to you — the EPS gap or the revenue beat?

slots.title: Post-Election AI Spending in the Headlines
slots.body:
After the midterms, several outlets describe investors weighing political resistance to AI spending and data centers — not a new regulation on the tape, but a policy story markets were already trading.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,579.42, up 1.1% on the session.

The S&P 500 finished at 7,376.86, up 0.3%.

The VIX — a gauge of expected stock volatility — fell 9.0% to 25.64.

That session tone sits alongside week-ahead commentary that major indexes had swung from election optimism into a technology-led drawdown tied to those same policy worries.

Gridlock limits what one party can pass alone; the discussion in the feed is about sentiment and capex timing, not a single bill number.

Where do you draw the line between election headlines and company-level AI demand?

slots.title: Iran Tensions Still in the Oil Story
slots.body:
Oil markets this week reacted in part to U.S. politics and the war in Iran — not a single new sanctions headline in the feed, but a geopolitical frame for energy prices.

Brent crude settled at $98.32, flat on the day (0.0%).

The U.S. Oil fund ($USO) closed at $148.41, up 0.1% on the session.

Coverage notes that Gulf states are still bracing for possible escalation even after the midterm vote shifted expectations for how long fighting might last.

Higher crude still shows up in household fuel costs in most states; Alaska’s state budget is an exception because it earns from local production.

Does your read on oil start with the barrel price or with headlines out of the Middle East?

slots.title: Chips rebound 6% as Nasdaq outpaces Dow
slots.body:
The Nasdaq Composite closed up 1.1% at 24,579.42.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.5% to 51,285.73 — a split tape between growth and blue chips.

Large semiconductor names led the upside:

- $TSM +6.3% to 375.44
- $ASML +5.0% to 1,424.75
- $NVDA +2.8% to 186.64

The Direxion 3x semiconductor bull fund $SOXL rose 12.5% to 45.97 on the session.

Coverage of the week’s technology decline pointed to macro fears around AI credit risk and political pushback on data-center buildouts after the midterms — not fresh earnings misses from the chip leaders.

Which large-cap name on your screen had the biggest Friday reversal?

slots.title: US cash session — Nov. 7, 2026
slots.body:
The S&P 500 finished up 0.3% at 7,376.86, gaining 23.13 points after trading between 7,369.55 and 7,444.20.
The benchmark held below its 52-week high of 7,844.52 from the data.

The Nasdaq Composite led US equities, up 1.1% to 24,579.42.
That +264.43-point session stood apart from the Dow, which lost 0.5% and closed at 51,285.73.

The Russell 2000 rose 0.9% to 2,754.11.
Small caps participated in the risk-on tilt that favored growth over the Dow’s 30 industrial names.

The CBOE Volatility Index fell 9.0% to 25.64, down 2.54 points from 28.18.
The session range ran from 23.47 to 27.76 — a softer close after a bruising week for technology in the headlines.

Semiconductors dominated the megacap leaderboard.
Taiwan Semiconductor $TSM rose 6.3% to 375.44.
ASML $ASML gained 5.0% to 1,424.75.
NVIDIA $NVDA added 2.8% to 186.64 on heavy volume of 179.3 million shares.
Intel $INTC, among the most active names, closed up 7.7% at 56.28.

Software and select consumer megacaps lagged the Nasdaq.
Salesforce $CRM fell 3.9% to 213.65.
Microsoft $MSFT was down 1.0% at 530.61.
Walmart $WMT lost 1.7% to 125.52.
Apple $AAPL slipped 0.5% to 342.37.

Johnson & Johnson $JNJ stood out on the plus side among defensives, up 1.4% to 276.22.
Alphabet $GOOGL rose 0.8% to 284.78.
Banks were slightly weaker: JPMorgan $JPM down 0.8% to 334.49, Bank of America $BAC down 0.7% to 49.42.

Berkshire Hathaway released results on the calendar: Class B EPS 10.33 versus 5.88 estimated, revenue about $105.6 billion versus about $101.0 billion estimated.
$BRK-B closed down 0.2% at 570.95; $BRK-A finished at 856,612.00.

In cross-asset markets, gold futures settled at 4,079.60, down 0.8%.
The US Oil Fund $USO edged up 0.1% to 148.41.
Brent crude $BZUSD was flat at 98.32.
The dollar-bullish fund $UUP rose 0.7% to 29.13 while EUR/USD slipped to 1.11.
Bitcoin $BTCUSD ticked up 0.1% to 75,840.42.

Treasury yields in the injected snapshot (dated 2026-11-05) showed the 10-year at 4.8% and the 2s10s spread at 0.38 percentage points — context for the session, not a same-day print in the feed.

Overnight and overseas, Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 6.0% at 57,434.77.
The FTSE 100 lost 1.0%.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 2.4% to 24,481.90 — a divergent global backdrop against the US chip-led bounce.

Among liquid advancers outside the megacap list, JFrog $FROG rose 35.3% to 100.98.
Firefly Aerospace $FLY gained 36.8% to 20.76.
On the downside, iRhythm $IRTC fell 30.7% to 90.22 and Karat Packaging $KRT lost 34.8% to 33.54.
No major US economic releases appeared in the session economic calendar in the injected data.

slots.title: October CPI lands Tuesday 8:30 a.m.
slots.body:
October CPI is on the calendar for Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 8:30 a.m.
ET.

Headline inflation is expected at 3.7% year-over-year, unchanged from the prior reading, and 0.3% month-over-month versus 0.6% last month.

Core inflation — prices minus food and energy — is estimated at 2.5% YoY and 0.2% MoM versus 0.3% prior.

The release measures what households paid for goods and services and is one of the main inputs markets use to read price pressure.

Which line do you watch first: headline, core, or the monthly rate?

slots.title: $CSCO and $AMAT report Wednesday
slots.body:
Wednesday, Nov. 12, brings two large-cap tech results.

$CSCO — Cisco Systems — carries a consensus of $1.32 EPS and roughly $18.1 billion in revenue.

$AMAT — Applied Materials — is modeled at $4.06 EPS and roughly $10.3 billion in revenue.

Cisco frames enterprise networking and security demand; Applied Materials reports on semiconductor equipment orders and backlog.

Both names report after the regular session closes on the 12th.

Networking or equipment — which print are you lining up for?

slots.title: PPI October due Friday 8:30 a.m.
slots.body:
Friday, Nov. 13, at 8:30 a.m.
ET: October producer price index.

PPI month-over-month is estimated at 0.4%, down from 1.3% the prior month.

PPI year-over-year is estimated at 6.1% versus 6.3% previously.

Core PPI MoM is estimated at 0.3% versus 0.7% prior; core PPI YoY is estimated at 4.9% versus 5.0%.

Producer prices track what businesses pay at the wholesale level — often read as an early read on pipeline costs before they reach consumer prices.

Do you treat PPI as a leading signal for CPI or as its own number?
